questions.q: In 1905 Einstein took Planck's energy lumps and made one bolder claim that Planck himself refused to make. What was it?
options: That atoms can only emit energy in discrete packets
That light itself travels through space as discrete particles, each carrying energy E = hf
That the speed of light is the same for all observers
That the energy of a light wave depends on its amplitude
questions.explanation: Planck quantised only the exchange of energy between atoms and still believed light itself was a continuous wave. Einstein went further and said light itself is made of indivisible photons, each carrying E = hf. That is the step he called 'very revolutionary'.

questions.q: Lenard pinned down four key behaviours of the photoelectric effect by 1902. Which one did the classical wave model actually predict correctly?
options: There is no time delay, even for very dim light
There is a threshold frequency below which no electrons are emitted
Brighter light of the same colour ejects more electrons
The kinetic energy of each electron depends only on frequency, not intensity
questions.explanation: The wave model fails on the no-delay, threshold-frequency, and energy-versus-frequency results, but it does correctly predict that brighter light ejects more electrons. In an exam, say the wave model fails on the other three, not all four.

questions.q: In Einstein's photon model, why is there a threshold frequency below which no electrons are emitted, no matter how bright the light?
options: Dim light cannot deliver photons fast enough to warm the metal
Each electron interacts with only one photon, so if hf is less than the work function no single photon can free it, and the photons cannot pool their energy
Low-frequency photons are reflected by the metal surface
Below the threshold the metal becomes positively charged and pulls electrons back
questions.explanation: An electron can absorb only one photon at a time, all or nothing. If hf is below the work function, no individual photon carries enough energy, so a billion weak photons still free nothing. Brighter just means more photons, not more energy each.

questions.q: What did Robert Millikan set out to do, and what did his ten years of work actually achieve?
options: He set out to confirm Einstein's photon, and proved light is purely a particle
He set out to disprove Einstein's equation, but instead measured a straight-line graph whose slope gave Planck's constant, confirming the equation
He set out to measure the electron's charge, and discovered the photoelectric effect
He set out to disprove Planck, and showed black-body radiation was continuous
questions.explanation: Millikan thought the photon was 'wholly untenable' and tried to measure the equation to death. His freshly cut surfaces gave perfectly straight, parallel stopping-voltage-versus-frequency lines whose slope yielded Planck's constant, confirming Einstein even while Millikan still rejected the photon idea.

questions.q: On a graph of maximum kinetic energy of photoelectrons against frequency, what does the slope of the line represent?
options: The work function of the metal
The threshold frequency
Planck's constant
The stopping voltage
questions.explanation: Comparing K_max = hf - W with y = mx + c, the slope is h. The line crosses the frequency axis at the threshold frequency f0 and the energy axis at -W. Einstein predicted this slope would equal the same h Planck had pulled out of the black-body problem.

questions.q: Einstein was awarded the 1921 Nobel Prize in Physics for which work?
options: Special relativity and E = mc^2
His discovery of the law of the photoelectric effect
Proving that atoms are real via Brownian motion
The Compton effect demonstrating photon momentum
questions.explanation: Students often guess relativity, but the citation reads 'for his discovery of the law of the photoelectric effect'. The committee was still uneasy about relativity and wanted something solid, which Millikan had measured to within about half a percent.

questions.q: From memory: state the two predictions the classical wave model makes about the photoelectric effect that turned out to be flatly false.
keyPoints: It predicts there is no hard threshold frequency: any colour of light should eventually work if it is bright enough or shone for long enough.
It predicts a measurable time delay at low intensity, as the electron slowly 'fills up like a bucket' until it has enough energy to escape.
Lenard observed neither: there was an absolute threshold frequency, and emission was instantaneous with no delay.
questions.explanation: If you recalled both the 'no threshold' and 'time delay' predictions and noted that Lenard observed neither, grade yourself Good or Easy.

questions.q: From memory, in your own words: state Einstein's photoelectric equation and explain why it is really just conservation of energy.
keyPoints: K_max = hf - W: the maximum kinetic energy equals the photon energy (hf) minus the work function W.
One photon hands all of its energy to one electron in a single collision.
The electron spends the work function W escaping the metal and keeps whatever is left over as kinetic energy: energy in = escape cost + energy out.
questions.explanation: The equation is conservation of energy applied to a single photon-electron collision. If you wrote K_max = hf - W and explained the energy bookkeeping, mark it Good or Easy.

questions.q: A metal has a work function of 1.67 eV. A photon of energy 2.92 eV strikes it. Find the maximum kinetic energy of the ejected photoelectron, in eV.
working: Because \(eV_s = K_{\max}\) and the energy is in eV, the stopping voltage reads straight across as \(1.25\,\mathrm{V}\).
questions.explanation: Straight application of K_max = hf - W. When energies are in eV, the stopping voltage equals the kinetic energy numerically, so V_s = 1.25 V.

questions.q: Light of frequency 7.06 x 10^14 Hz strikes a metal surface. Using Planck's constant h = 6.63 x 10^-34 J s, find the energy of one photon, in joules.
questions.explanation: Direct use of the Planck-Einstein relation E = hf. Dividing by 1.6 x 10^-19 C converts this to about 2.92 eV, the photon energy used in the previous question.
